name: std::string append() concatenation (vs ostringstream and operator+)
listed_description: Building a string with repeated std::string::append() calls, benchmarked against operator+, std::ostringstream and std::format().
claim_text: append() fastest at about 75 ms for 10 million iterations; ostringstream about 1,435 ms.
book_benchmark: 10 million concatenations of two one-char strings with a separator, one timed run with chrono, GCC 15.2 -O2, Debian VM (Linux 6.17), CPU not stated. operator+ 175 ms, format 929 ms. Author says Apple Clang showed append close to operator+ and MSVC slower. Companion repo PacktPublishing/C-23-STL-Cookbook-Second-Edition showed only Chap01 to Chap06 folders when checked, so code for this chapter may not be public.
found_in: book: C++23 STL Cookbook, 2nd ed. (2026), ch. 7 Strings and Formatting, recipe Concatenate strings, section Benchmarks

name: std::format() string building (vs ostringstream)
listed_description: C++20 std::format() used to build a string, said to give iostream-style type safety without the stream overhead.
claim_text: format() about 930 ms vs about 1,435 ms for ostringstream over 10 million iterations; significantly faster than ostringstream.
book_benchmark: Same concatenation loop as the append() entry: 10 million iterations, GCC 15.2 -O2, Debian VM, CPU not stated, single run. format slower than append (75 ms) and operator+ (175 ms). Companion repo PacktPublishing/C-23-STL-Cookbook-Second-Edition showed only Chap01 to Chap06 folders when checked, so code for this chapter may not be public.
found_in: book: C++23 STL Cookbook, 2nd ed. (2026), ch. 7 Strings and Formatting, recipe Concatenate strings, section Benchmarks and Why the performance discrepancy

name: std::print / std::println (C++23)
listed_description: C++23 print functions built on the format library that bypass iostream for console and file output.
claim_text: far more efficient than using format with cout; performance and code size comparable to printf().
book_benchmark: No measurement given; qualitative claim only.
found_in: book: C++23 STL Cookbook, 2nd ed. (2026), ch. 7 Strings and Formatting, recipe Print strings with std::print and std::println, introduction

name: C++17 parallel execution policies (std::execution::par / par_unseq) for std::sort and std::transform
listed_description: Passing std::execution::par or par_unseq to standard algorithms so the library spreads work over CPU cores.
claim_text: sort of 20 million values: 835 ms sequential, 158 ms with par, 152 ms with par_unseq.
book_benchmark: 20 million random unsigned values, std::sort and std::transform (multiply by 2), single runs timed with chrono steady_clock, MSVC on a 6-core Intel i7, flags not stated. transform: 8.74 ms no policy, 10.9 ms seq, 6.2 ms par, 5.99 ms par_unseq. Book notes GCC support is poor and Apple Clang lacks it. Companion repo PacktPublishing/C-23-STL-Cookbook-Second-Edition showed only Chap01 to Chap06 folders when checked, so code for this chapter may not be public.
found_in: book: C++23 STL Cookbook, 2nd ed. (2026), ch. 9 Concurrency and Parallelism, recipe Run STL algorithms in parallel with execution policies, sections How to do it and How it works

name: std::string_view (vs std::string for read-only text)
listed_description: Non-owning view of character data, passed instead of std::string to avoid copying and allocation.
claim_text: smaller and more efficient than std::string; avoids the copying and storage cost.
book_benchmark: No measurement given; qualitative claim only.
found_in: book: C++23 STL Cookbook, 2nd ed. (2026), ch. 7 Strings and Formatting, recipe Use string_view as a lightweight string object, introduction
